segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we're looking a bit at possession now, no? And how we express that in Spanish. Now in English we use

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: possessive words, my, your, his, her, much more than we do in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So it's something we want to look out for. We already saw an example actually, for example how we would say "I responded him the mail" rather than "I responded to his mail".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Another example would be how we refer to body parts in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you don't say in Spanish, for example, "my leg hurts". You say "it hurts me the leg".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Doler, doler is to hurt.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say firstly "it hurts me" from doler? It hurts me.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me dolo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It hurts me.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No, me...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I want you to divide the sentence up and to take control of it. No guessing. It hurts me.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Dole.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. It would be dole, but the "o" splits. So this is an error that's not a problem, you thought it through and you got to dole, huh? But the "o" splits here.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: So, me duele.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me duele. Good. Me duele. So you don't say in Spanish "my leg hurts", mi pierna duele, you don't say that. You say "it hurts me the leg". It hurts me the leg. So leg is pierna,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: how would you say "my leg hurts"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me duele la pierna.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Me duele la pierna. If you want to say "my leg doesn't hurt anymore", you can just use "more" for "anymore". So what was "more" again?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Más.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Más. So, "my leg doesn't hurt anymore"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No me duele la pierna más.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Now the noun pain is dolor, dolor.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Dolor.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you want to say "I have a headache", you can just say "I have pain of head", dolor de cabeza, dolor de cabeza. So how would that be, "I have a headache"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tengo dolor de cabeza.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Tengo dolor de cabeza. Good. "I had", "I was having" pain of head, so the line in the past?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tenía dolor de cabeza.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Tenía dolor de cabeza. And of course we can also say me duele la cabeza or me dolía la cabeza. This would be another way of saying it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So just as we can say dolor de cabeza to say headache, the ache of the head,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: if we want to say "José's house", "María's house", in Spanish we would say "the house of María", "the house of José". So how would you say "the house of José", José's house?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La casa de José.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "we are going to José's house"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vamos a la casa de José.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Vamos a la casa de José. What if you wanted to say "we are going to María's party", "we are going to María's party"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vamos a la fie...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: That's correct.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vamos a la fiesta de María.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. Vamos a la fiesta de María. Very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was "nobody"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nadie.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Nadie. And "nobody else" or "nobody more"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Nadie más.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "I didn't speak with anybody else in María's party. I didn't speak with anyone else in María's party, I only spoke with you." So let's start from the beginning. "I didn't speak"...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No hablé...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...with anybody else...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...con nadie más...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...in María's party...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...en... en la fiesta de María...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No hablé con nadie más en la fiesta de María. "I only spoke with you." Now "only" or "just", that we say a lot in English "I just spoke with you", "I only spoke with you", in Spanish is solo, solo. So, "I only spoke with you", speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablaste...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I only spoke with you. Don't let it blend together.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablé contigo solo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, or more naturally might be solo hablé contigo. But solo at the end there, it's fine, it just sounds more emphatic. You might want to be emphatic here. No hablé con nadie más en la fiesta de María, solo hablé contigo. Hablé solo contigo. Hablé contigo solo.
